content.title: Germany reacts prudently to Russia’s aggression
content.lead: Following the attack in Leipzig, the German government is closing two Russian facilities. It demonstrates resolve without overreacting. However, a statement by Chancellor Friedrich Merz leaves a bitter aftertaste.

content.text: You are reading an excerpt from the newsletter «Der andere Blick am Morgen» (The Other View in the Morning), today by Jonas Hermann, NZZ Germany editor. Subscribe to the newsletter for free. Not resident in Germany? Find out more here.

Sovereignty sometimes also means restraint: an insulted party should not retaliate, and a provoked one should not overreact – if only to avoid stooping to the level of the aggressor. In this sense, the German government reacted appropriately when it announced on Tuesday evening its response to the attack that targeted Leipzig Airport in early August. Russia is highly likely responsible. A drone equipped with explosives was apparently intended to hit a Ukrainian cargo plane there.

In response, Germany will close the Russian House. It is located in the heart of Berlin and is officially a cultural institution. In reality, Russian intelligence services likely use it. In addition, Russia must also close its Consulate General in Bonn. Germany also intends to take tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. Russia circumvents Western sanctions with the scrap ships of this fleet. Germany still has room for improvement to prevent this unfortunate spectacle as much as possible.

The government thus draws lines but does not overreact. This is prudent. Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s statement a week ago was somewhat less prudent: «They will pay for it,» he declared regarding those who commissioned the attack in Leipzig. Merz sounded like the hero in an action movie, but his strong words do not quite fit the prudent reaction that he had his Interior and Foreign Ministers announce on Tuesday evening.

Russia’s actions against Europe have one thing in common: they generally cannot be unequivocally attributed to Russia. Cyberattacks, parcel bombs, drones that paralyze airports, systematic disinformation – all of this affects Germany’s sovereignty and that of its neighboring states. However, Russia can always deny all of this, which is, of course, part of the calculation. Nevertheless, the German government on Tuesday held Russia responsible for the failed attack on Leipzig Airport.

This is also appropriate for two reasons: First, politicians are not judges who must always decide in favor of the accused in cases of doubt. Second, the overall view of the many hybrid actions against Ukraine’s supporters allows no other conclusion than that Russia is behind them.

content.title: AfD and BSW united in error

content.text: Germany’s room for maneuver is limited because its intelligence services can do less and are permitted to do much less than, for example, their American counterparts. The capabilities of the Bundeswehr are also limited. For example, drone defense in Germany is a nascent discipline.

However, political reasons also limit the government’s options. The AfD and BSW invert reality: Politicians from these parties claim that Germany is pursuing an aggressive course against Russia. In this particular reality, the NATO states are ultimately to blame for the war in Ukraine. Russia’s campaign is thus – more or less – reinterpreted as an act of self-defense. Its war crimes are transformed in this worldview into a necessary evil that, these politicians claim, the West provoked unnecessarily.

This can only be explained by the fact that AfD leader Tino Chrupalla seriously said of Russian strongman Vladimir Putin: «He has done nothing to me.» Germany as an aggressor, Merz as a warmonger – this is what it sounds like not only from the far right but also from the far left. An overreaction to the attack in Leipzig would only have unnecessarily fueled Russia apologists.

newestTopComments.text: Anyone who thinks they can get away scot-free by kowtowing to a dictator is sorely mistaken. Dictators only speak the language of strength; the sooner you speak or act accordingly, the less damage, suffering, and misery you will suffer. Freedom doesn't come for free.

Shortly before the crucial election in Saxony-Anhalt, the Merz government has discovered Russia as the perfect bogeyman: an alleged attack, numerous hypotheses, no publicly presented evidence so far – but already diplomatic escalation and the appropriate campaign ammunition against the AfD are following. What has become all too familiar since the pandemic seems to be becoming a political tactic once again: fear breeds allegiance, doubt becomes suspect, and the very opposition that is pushing for diplomacy and an end to support for Ukraine can be branded as Moscow's fifth column...
